newsitem.title: CANADA: Martin says confidence behind higher unemployment.
newsitem.headline: Martin says confidence behind higher unemployment.

text.p: Canadians' increased confidence in the economy was behind the rise in unemployment in October, Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Friday.

"It is unfortunate, very much so, that the unemployment rate went up. But I think you have to take a look at the reason. And the reason is increasing confidence in the Canadian economy," Martin told reporters on his way to a cabinet meeting.
Martin said that as more Canadians felt better about the economy, they were more likely to start looking for jobs. Canada's unemployment rate measures only people seeking jobs.
Martin said more people seeking work meant that the labor force would grow faster than the number of new jobs, thus bringing higher unemployment rates for a while.

"I think that the unemployment rate will come down more slowly because as people gain more and more confidence, as the economic recovery takes hold, then they're going to come back into the work force," Martin said.
Canada's economy created 42,000 jobs in October, but the unemployment rate edged up to 10.0 percent from 9.9 percent as the number of people looking for jobs outpaced job creation.

Despite a series of aggressive interest rate cuts by the Bank of Canada, the country's unemployment rate remained stubbornly high in the first 10 months of 1996, reflecting sluggish domestic demand in an economy relying mostly on export growth.
-- Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau (613) 235-6745
